stories.text: Love. It's a many-splendored thing, except when it isn't. And in this case, it was a very criminal thing. Hawaii News Now reports a Kula woman is one of three people who have pleaded guilty in a $9 million international romance fraud scheme that went after mostly older Americans. 53-year-old Amanda Joy Opoku-Boeshe pleaded guilty October 20th to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. stories.headline: Pest experts question state's $1 million invasive species contract

stories.text: Some pest experts are bugged about a state contract, apparently with good reason. Civil Beat reports Hawaiʻi signed a vague $1 million contract in June with Shizen Consulting Management, a five-year-old engineering firm, to figure out which imports are most likely to carry new invasive species into our islands. Pest management professionals told Civil Beat the assessment is an exorbitant waste of money and that the contractors aren't qualified to do the job. The state has spent tens of millions of dollars fighting invasive species, and critics say the money needs to go directly to those fighting them, not to hear more people talk.

stories.text: Originally from South America, where they had a lot of competition, little fire ants hitchhiked to Florida, and then to the Big Island, likely on plants. And without their normal competitors, they multiplied to unbelievable numbers and spread to other islands. They infest plants, trees, beaches, playgrounds, and yards, and create super colonies, which makes them difficult to avoid and easy to spread. The colonies are moved with potted plants, gardening supplies, yard waste, building materials, and vehicles. They sting, and it hurts, leaving behind an itchy, painful rash that lasts for days or weeks. Pets and livestock are also at risk. stories.headline: Kīhei motorcyclist killed in collision with SUV on Pi’ilani Highway
stories.summary: A 37-year-old Kīhei man died when his motorcycle collided with an SUV turning left, and the 18-year-old driver was arrested for third-degree negligent injury, marking Maui County's 11th traffic fatality of 2026.
stories.text: There was horror on Maui roads this past weekend. A 37-year-old Kīhei man died on his motorcycle Friday night. Police say the man was riding south on P'ilani Highway shortly after 7.30 p.m. when his Harley-Davidson collided with an SUV turning left from Kaonauulu Street. The SUV's 18-year-old driver was arrested for third-degree negligent injury and later released pending further investigation. The motorcyclist was wearing a helmet, and police have not determined whether speed, drugs, or alcohol were factors. His death marks Maui County's 11th traffic fatality of the year, compared with 14 at this time last year.

Several large vessels are anchored close to shore. The monstrous explosion is powerful enough to wipe out a small city. The debris is sent flying more than half a mile into the bay as the ships are engulfed in a thick cloud of dust. Watch as two surveillance blimps are blown out of the sky. Cameras mounted aboard the ships record the destruction. The shock waves are mighty enough to rip through steel walls. Heavy radar equipment is sent flying. A life-size mannequin placed on the deck of one ship is blasted off its feet with frightening force. More than a minute later fragments of red hot metal continue to rain down. Smoke clears revealing that somehow the ships have stayed afloat, but they are severely damaged. This simulation serves as an ominous example of the deadly and devastating power of nuclear weapons.

stories.headline: Seabird fallout season: what to do if you find a bird
stories.summary: October through December is peak fallout season when young seabirds are confused by lights, and residents are asked to call a hotline and reduce outdoor lighting.
stories.text: If you find a bird on the ground that looks lost, it may need your help. Maui Now reports October through December is peak fallout season, when young seabirds leave their burrows and head out to sea for the first time. They include juvenile ʻUaʻu kani, or wedge-tailed shearwaters, and the endangered ʻUaʻu, or Hawaiian petrol. The birds navigate by the moon and stars and bright artificial lights can confuse them, sending them into buildings and power lines or leaving them grounded and exhausted. The Maui Nui Seabird Recovery Project asks you to call its hotline if you find one, and the state DLNR is urging everyone to cut back on outdoor lighting.

In the second quarter, Molokaʻi scores a direct snap to Ikua Hanchett for a 7-yard TD run. The extra point was blocked at the half. Hāna 7, Molokaʻi 6. Third quarter, no scoring. Fourth quarter, Hāna, a 35-yard fumble recovery touchdown by Nāʻau Lind. Extra point is blocked. It's 13 to 6. Hāna. In the fourth quarter, Makena Kahele to Jafeth Kahuluaʻa, 18-yard TD pass, late in the fourth quarter. Two-point conversion is good by Ikua Hanna. Mocchi, Molokaʻi wins 14 to 13 on the road in Hāna. Great job, Molokaʻi Football. We look forward to your home game on October 17th where you will face the Hāna Dragons again. And we have to wait and see on the standings regarding a playoff for the 8-man championship. Lānaʻi is at Hāna this Friday night and we'll look forward to that result. We will see you on October 17th as we host the Hauna Dragons in a big game for Molokai Football. You can get your tickets at GoFans.co.
